questions.question: What is JSX and how does it work?
questions.title: Jsx Explained
questions.direct_answer:
JSX is a syntax extension that looks like HTML but compiles to function calls — `
Hi
` becomes `React.createElement('div', {className: 'x'}, 'Hi')`, which returns a plain object describing the element. It's sugar over create-element calls, not a template language.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    J[JSX you write] --> T[Babel/compilers]
    T --> C[React.createElement calls]
    C --> E[element objects: type props key]
    E --> R[renderer - react-dom]
    R --> D[real DOM nodes]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The element tree (what JSX ultimately produces): each createElement call returns an immutable element object — `{type, props, key}`. Elements are descriptions, not instances: React can discard and recreate them cheaply on every render because they're just data. The renderer (react-dom for web, react-native's renderer for mobile) turns element trees into host instances (DOM nodes, native views).

The children shapes (the edge interviewers probe): children can be a string, an element, an array of elements, or a function (render props). Arrays carry the key requirement — React matches array children by key across renders, and unkeyed children get positional matching, which breaks on reorder/insert.

The compile-time optimizations (modern depth): the new React Compiler (React Forget) analyzes components at build time and auto-inserts memoization — the manual useMemo/useCallback discipline becomes unnecessary for most code. JSX itself is also being optimized by tools like Solid and Svelte's compilers into fine-grained updates, but React's model stays: describe the tree, diff it, apply it.
